data.title: Hričovské Podhradie – a castle hill occupied long before Hričov Castle
data.excerpt: Hričov Castle has a long history that began well before the stone medieval castle was built. Finds of Lusatian, Púchov culture and Slavic pottery from the castle hill and from the cave beside it show that the rock was occupied from the Early Iron Age right through to the Middle Ages.
data.metaTitle: Hričov – a castle hill occupied before the castle
data.metaDescription: The castle hill at Hričov was occupied long before the stone castle – finds of the Lusatian and Púchov cultures reach back to the Early Iron Age.

children.text: Hričov Castle has a long and rich history reaching back well before the stone medieval castle arose here. Archaeological finds discovered as early as the end of the 1940s document an occupation of the castle hill far older than the Middle Ages and the modern period. The first of them were handed over by A. Petrovský-Šichman as early as 1947 to Prof. V. Budinský-Krička, who assigned them to the Early Iron Age. Similar material was also discovered by O. Šedo in the locality known as Komíny (spot height 532), which lies to the north of the castle. All these finds can be assigned to the framework of the Lusatian culture, which in the Late Bronze Age to the Early Iron Age represents the occupation of northern Slovakia. Most of the material from the castle hill belongs to the Púchov culture. It is represented above all by fragments of vessels decorated with vertical grooving, which is typical precisely of the pottery of the Púchov culture of the late La Tène period. To these can also be assigned fragments of large clay storage vessels in which the inhabitants of northern Slovakia of the time kept their food supplies. The finds of Púchov culture pottery of the late La Tène to the early Roman period discovered in the area of Hričovské Podhradie are proof that this area was already continuously occupied at the end of the old and the beginning of the new era. Material of the Púchov culture came to light on the castle hill, which also bears the name Mikov kopec, in 1949 as well. A number of finds of Púchov culture pottery from the castle hill were also handed over to the Považie Museum by the museum's long-standing collaborator Štefan Meliš from Považská Bystrica, and most of them again belong to the sphere of the Púchov culture, chiefly of the late La Tène period and the early Roman period. In 1961 František Kvasník found iron tongs and a fragment of a quernstone in the cave beside the castle, which can likewise be assigned to the sphere of Púchov culture material. The iron tongs became at that time the very first find of their kind in the whole of northern Slovakia and therefore also became part of the display of the Púchov culture in Púchov.

children.text: One of the most recent surveys of the grounds of Hričov Castle was carried out by members of the archaeological circle from Považská Bystrica on 25 August 1993, when the cave below the castle, from which the iron tongs come, was also examined. The cave is about 15 m long, and in front of its upper opening a pit measuring about 6 × 3.5 m and some 5 m deep had been dug, which cut through all the occupation layers on the castle hill. The pit was dug by a local man, Kabašta, who came here regularly and evidently also carried archaeological finds away. From the individual layers it was possible at least partly to reconstruct the find situation on the castle hill. In the lowest layer there was material of the late La Tène period – that is, of the Púchov culture; in the middle of the cut there were already finds of Slavic pottery, and in the upper layers medieval pottery. As the individual occupation layers built up, the space in front of the cave filled in as well, and so some finds found their way into its interior too.

The first Slavic pottery on the castle hill was discovered by A. Petrovský-Šichman as early as 1947 and then by F. Kvasník in 1959. In 1949 A. Petrovský-Šichman opened the first trench at the site of Mikov kopec – the castle hill, in which, besides sherds of the Púchov culture, fragments of Slavic pottery were also found, as well as a unique stone spindle whorl from a spindle for winding yarn. In 1969, too, pupils of the Building Construction training school found in the cave of the castle crag pottery from several periods of the Middle Ages, dated to the 10th – 11th century and then to the 12th – 13th century. Among the finds handed over to the Považie Museum in Žilina by Š. Meliš there were, besides older material, also fragments of vessels of the 9th – 10th century and then of the 10th – 11th century.

The repeatedly attested evidence of occupation of the castle hill before the castle itself arose – it is mentioned only in 1254, when King Béla IV granted it to Toluš, son of Farkaš – speaks clearly for the view that an older fortification could have stood here far earlier than the middle of the 13th century, and only afterwards could the medieval castle arise. Finds of medieval pottery are also mentioned in the report of Prof. V. Budinský-Krička on the publication of the assemblage of material acquired by the State Archaeological Institute in 1946 – 1947. It thus seems that occupation of the castle hill continued without interruption in the following periods as well, for which written sources are already available. As a counterpart to the medieval castle one may also add the small fortification above Dolný Hričov in the locality known as Dúbravy. This smaller fortification lies on the crown of the hill, just above the junction of the Váh-region royal road with its shorter branch running through Ovčiarsko to Žilina. The western foot of the hill bears the name “Imramovec”, from which A. Petrovský-Šichman inferred that the term derives from the name of St Emmeram, to whom the oldest Christian building in the territory of present-day Slovakia, in Pribina's Nitrava, was dedicated. Because the Hričov estate was already the property of the bishopric of Nitra at the beginning of the 13th century (1208), a church dedicated to St Emmeram may have stood here as well. The latest contribution to the occupation of the area is the find of Slavic pottery of the 9th and perhaps also the 10th century on the site of the construction of the VITACO company's production hall. These finds, too, support the assumption of long-term Slavic occupation of the area before the castle itself, the building of which began only much later, in the middle of the 13th century.
